overview.text: Mathematical induction is a deductive proof method for showing that a statement holds for every integer from a chosen starting value onward. It has two linked parts: verify the statement at the starting value (the base case), then show that whenever it holds at an arbitrary value k, it must also hold at k+1 (the inductive step). Each case therefore passes the result to the next, like climbing an endless staircase. Unlike spotting a pattern in a few examples, induction gives a logical proof that the claim continues indefinitely. It is useful for results about number patterns and formulas; in strong induction, the proof may use all earlier cases, not just the immediately previous one.

key_facts.text: The starting value need not be 1; induction can prove a claim for integers from any specified starting point onward.
In the inductive step, assume the claim for an arbitrary k in range, then prove it for k+1; this assumption is the inductive hypothesis.
Checking several initial cases may suggest a pattern, but by itself does not prove that the pattern holds for every later case.
Mathematical induction is deductive reasoning, distinct from scientific induction, which draws general ideas from observations.
Strong induction is a related form: to prove the next case, the inductive step may assume the claim holds for all earlier cases in range.
